subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
passage:
Monday: After reading a news story about leaked company data, Vijay, head of a small design agency, emailed the team: 'No AI tools of any kind, effective today.' People nodded, a bit stunned.

Two weeks later: Deadlines were tight. Saurabh, a copywriter, quietly opened a personal account on a phone and pasted in a client's draft brief to get a rewrite. Others did the same and kept quiet; nobody wanted to be the one to tell Vijay.

Six weeks later: A client spotted a line in a document that matched text shared only in a private brief. Vijay learned that half the team had been using personal accounts with client files. At a meeting Vijay asked, 'Why didn't anyone tell me?' A designer answered, 'You said no. We still had deadlines.'

qa.a: It said, 'No AI tools of any kind, effective today.'

qa.q: What was Vijay afraid of when sending the email?
qa.a: Vijay was afraid of leaking company data, after reading a news story about a leak.

qa.q: What other approach could Vijay have used instead of a full ban?
qa.a: Vijay could have written a clear policy on approved tools and what data never goes in, so people had a safe way to work and no reason to hide it.

qa.q: How did the ban look to Saurabh and the others?
qa.a: It felt unworkable with deadlines pressing, so they used personal accounts quietly and stayed silent, since nobody wanted to tell Vijay.

grounding: Shows a manager forbidding all AI use out of fear, while staff quietly use personal accounts, creating hidden risk that a clear policy could have prevented.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
passage: Chaitanya, you asked why I fought so hard for an AI policy instead of a ban. When I was twenty-five, my manager at a bank's tech centre got scared after reading one article about leaks. He sent an email: all AI tools forbidden, full stop. No explanation, no alternative. Did people stop? No. Half my team kept using the tools on their personal phones and home laptops, pasting in code and sometimes customer queries to get work done faster. Nobody talked about it, because it was forbidden. Six months later, an audit found client data in a personal chat account. That was the real leak, and the ban had pushed people into it. So when I became a manager, your Sonali ma'am wrote a clear policy instead: what's allowed, with which tools, and what never goes in.

qa.q: Where was the client data found?
qa.a: In a personal chat account, found by an audit six months later.

qa.q: What might Sonali's manager have felt when he sent the ban?
qa.a: He was scared after reading about leaks and wanted to feel safe quickly, so a total ban seemed the simplest answer.

qa.q: What choice could the manager have made instead of the ban?
qa.a: He could have written a clear policy naming safe tools and data rules, so people worked in the open instead of hiding.

qa.q: How might the client whose data leaked be affected?
qa.a: The client's private information ended up in a personal account, a breach of trust caused by hidden workarounds.

grounding: It shows a manager who bans all AI use out of fear, so staff secretly use personal accounts and create the leak a clear policy might have prevented.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
passage:
Preeti had banned every AI tool in the insurance team the week after a conference talk on data risks. 'Too dangerous. No exceptions,' her email said.
In March the quarter-end deadline hit. Shankar had forty claim letters to rewrite by Friday, and the office was short three people. At 11 p.m., alone at home, he pasted the letters, with customers' names and policy numbers, into a free chatbot on his personal account. It saved him six hours. He told nobody; it was forbidden.
In May a customer called, furious: parts of her claim letter had turned up in a public forum post about chatbot leaks. The investigation traced it to Shankar's account. Sitting across from Preeti, he said quietly, 'Everyone was doing it. We just couldn't say so.'

qa.q: How many claim letters did Shankar have to rewrite?
What might Shankar have been feeling at 11 p.m.?
qa.a: He was probably exhausted and pressured, anxious to meet the deadline, and uneasy about doing something forbidden.

qa.q: What approach could Preeti have taken instead of the ban?
qa.a: An approved tool with clear rules about removing names and policy numbers, so people under pressure had a safe, open option.
Parts of her private claim letter appeared in a public post, which left her angry and exposed.

grounding: It shows a manager forbidding all AI use out of fear, so staff secretly use personal accounts and create a leak a clear, safe policy might have prevented.
